tagline: Follow the Little Muskingum past covered crossings built and rebuilt
intro: Ohio’s Covered Bridge Scenic Byway follows State Route 26 between Woodsfield and Marietta, beside the Little Muskingum River for much of the drive. The road climbs through Graysville and follows stream valleys through hilly country in Wayne National Forest. The Forest Service presents this National Forest Scenic Byway as a tour of river scenery and history, with ten marked stops interpreting 35 miles. The river follows a tight, meandering course southwest through hill country, remaining within eight miles of the Ohio River.

The Marietta–Woodsfield road entered the state highway system in 1912 as SR 389, then became SR 26 in 1923. Its covered crossings predate those numbers: Rollin Meredith built Hune Bridge in 1879. Rinard Bridge dates to 1876, but a flash flood destroyed it in 2004 and a replacement followed in 2006. SR 26 was extended north of Woodsfield in 1937, so today’s numbered highway continues beyond the byway corridor.

Start at Woodsfield and drive south through Graysville toward the river. Continue through Rinard Mills, then Wingett Run and Dart, with their nearby covered bridges. Closer to Marietta, Hildreth Bridge stands off SR 26 above the Little Muskingum. The final approach crosses Duck Creek and passes beneath I-77 before entering Marietta.

moments.title: Wingett Run
moments.text: Near Wingett Run, the Rinard Covered Bridge marks a crossing rebuilt after a flood. The original 1876 bridge used a Smith truss and was built by the Smith Bridge Company of Toledo, with H. H. Townsend credited for the work. It was also called Hendershott’s Ford Bridge. A flash flood destroyed the structure on September 18, 2004; rebuilding followed in 2006. The crossing is northeast of Wingett Run on County Road 406, spanning the Little Muskingum. The community takes its name from a nearby stream named for Jacob Wingett, an early settler in the region.

moments.title: Dart
moments.text: Northeast of Dart, Hune Covered Bridge crosses the Little Muskingum on a single wooden span. Local bridge builder Rollin Meredith erected it in 1879 and used the Long-truss design, a complicated form with few surviving examples. The bridge was named for the Hune family. Its metal roof and vertical siding enclose the crossing, while cut-stone abutments support it at the ends. The bridge entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1976 for its local history and construction. Near Dart, Archers Fork joins the Little Muskingum, adding another tributary to the river followed by this road.
moments.notice: Hune Bridge has a metal roof, vertical siding and cut-stone abutments.

moments.title: Hildreth Covered Bridge
moments.text: Hildreth Covered Bridge took a decade to build: work extended from 1871 to 1881, with the largest share completed in 1878. Its builder’s identity is unknown. Also called Hills Covered Bridge and Lafaber’s Mill Bridge, it historically carried Hills Bridge Road over the Little Muskingum. The single wooden span uses a Howe truss supported on cut-stone abutments and piers. A metal roof, vertical siding and battens at the portals complete the structure. Its National Register recognition in 1978 acknowledged both the bridge’s role in local history and its historically significant construction.
moments.notice: The wooden span rests on stone supports and has a metal roof and vertical siding.
